The Adventures

of

a Japanese Doll.

A Picture Story told by

Henry Mayer.

London  
Grant Richards.  
New York: E. P. Dutton & Co.  
1901.

​

Armitage & Ibbetson, Limited,  
Printers,  
Bradford, England.

​

**Contents.**

1.  Ting-a-Ling’s Birthday.
2.  Who Yum-Yum was, and how she made her a Frock.
3.  Who Ah-Kymo was, and how she taught her to Dance.
4.  The jealous Chin-Chins.
5.  Ting-a-Ling becomes discontented.
6.  The Dream of the Wonderful Sunflower.
7.  The Dream of the Japanese Moon.
8.  The Man of Snow tries to comfort her with a Little Sermon.
9.  The Epic of the White Clouds.
10.  The Results of Carelessness and Malice.
11.  The Pansies weep for Ting-a-Ling.
12.  The Explosion.
13.  Ting-a-Ling disturbs a Game of Croquet.
14.  Ting-a-Ling gets a View from a German Chimney Pot.
15.  The Sphynx in the Desert.
16.  They catch a good, obliging Camel.
17.  They meet Two Little Foolish Blackamoors.
18.  Ting-a-Ling and her American Friend astonish the Squaw.
19.  Ting-a-Ling goes on a Fishing Expedition.
20.  Ting-a-Ling and Mr. Stork converse pleasantly in Mid-air.
21.  She stands in fear of the Village Boys.
22.  She explores every Nook and Cranny of the Swiss Mountains.
23.  She thinks deeply in the Stern of a Venetian Gondola.
24.  She joins the Merry-Makers in the Carnival.
25.  From Venice to the Black Forest.
26.  In Holland she skips with the Best of Them.
27.  Lucile and Auguste are baffled by Mr. Stork.
28.  Ting-a-Ling distinguishes Herself in the Highlands.
29.  What Happened in Chelsea.
30.  It all ends happily.

​

Ting-a-Ling's Birthday.

**Ting-a-Ling’s Birthday.**

​

I.

Ting-a-ling was a doll, and she was born in old Japan on a fine spring morning. Her father was the great Chung-Wah, a maker of toys and things that are odd or pretty, and who therefore enjoys the respectful affection of every Japanese child.

There was no reason why she should be born on one day rather than another; but, as I wish to be accurate, I will tell how and why it happened then.

Chung-Wah had been squatting on his mat since early morning making a coat of armour for the warlike son of the Mikado, when turning round he saw the doll I am telling you about lying patiently on her back with her eyes wide open, just waiting for his finishing touches.

Chung-Wah flung away his tools and looked about for his paint brushes.

“O Ting-a-ling!” said the great Chung-Wah, who was a poet in his way, “you are graceful and slim as a willow reed, and I will touch your cheeks with the bloom of the young almond blossoms!” He waved his brush gracefully in the air and painted her cheeks a delicate pink, so that she became the dearest and sweetest doll of old Japan.

​

Who Yum-Yum was, and how she made her a Frock.

**Who Yum-Yum was, and how she made her a Frock.**

​

II.

Now Chung-Wah had two beautiful daughters. Yum-Yum, the eldest, was betrothed to a youth who hunted butterflies by day, and spent the hours after sunset in fastening them on to paper lanterns. It is very difficult to do this without spoiling or tarnishing the gold and sapphire colour of their wings; so that this youth, betrothed to Yum-Yum, was occasionally a little sad, and a little thoughtful. But Yum-Yum would cheer him up by saying, “If the gold and the sapphire dust falls off their wings, what then? I will embroider blue and gold butterflies that will never fade on my little embroidery frame,” for Yum-Yum was very clever with her needle at her embroidery frame.

When she saw what a masterpiece of a doll Ting-a-ling was, she said, “O Ting-a-ling, your cheeks are like the almond blossom, and I will embroider you a beautiful gown all covered with flowers.”

So Ting-a-ling became the most beautiful and the best dressed dollie in old Japan.

​

Who Ah-Kymo was, and how she taught her to Dance.

**Who Ah-Kymo was, and how she taught her to Dance.**

​

III.

Ah-Kymo was the great Chung-Wah’s second daughter. She used to sit on the grass in her father’s garden and sing a song to the moon, or the spring, or the clouds. Or she would dance a graceful slow dance in honour of the westerly wind or the summer rain.

Her songs were a never-ending delight to herself and to many who, passing under the wall of her father’s garden, stopped to listen and to praise.

Now when Ah-Kymo saw the robe her sister had worked for Ting-a-ling, she said: “I will teach her a song I have just made to the gold fish in the lake at the foot of the garden, and I will teach her to dance like the petals of the blossoms when they fall on the green grass from the trees overhead: and many other things will I teach her.”

So all through the spring and summer Ting-a-ling learned first to walk, then to skip, then to dance. She also learned to sing, to speak, and think. She might even have learnt to argue, only in Japan people never do that; they only turn their eyes down and smile.

​

The jealous Chin-Chins.

**The jealous Chin-Chins.**

​

IV.

And now I must admit that all the Japanese chin-chins (they are Japanese spaniels, you know), who were once the family pets, became jealous of Ting-a-ling. “Bow-wow!” said the oldest, “you doll-child! All day long Yum-Yum bends over her frame embroidering flowers on satin to make a dress for you. When I pull the hem of her gown she doesn’t even notice me.”

“Bow-wow-wow!” said the second chin-chin, “before you came, Ting-a-ling, Ah-Kymo used to throw pebbles along the garden paths for me to run after; but now she is always busy teaching you to dance or skip, and even when I come running up with a stick in my mouth she hardly looks at me!”

“Bow-wow! Bow-wow!” chimed in a shriller voice, “was there ever such impudence seen in all Japan? We three chin-chins were the pets and darlings of this house; but since you’ve come, you naughty Ting-a-ling, we count for nothing!”

Ting-a-ling answered nothing, but smiled most wisely, for she knew, being a wise doll, that she would not stay for ever in Chung-Wah’s house to blight the happiness of those three misguided chin-chins.

​

Ting-a-Ling becomes discontented.

**Ting-a-Ling becomes discontented.**

​

V.

Now as the summer months went by the days grew shorter and colder. Chung-Wah’s eldest daughter had to leave her embroidery frame to warm the tips of her little fingers; and the youngest daughter picked up her Japanese guitar and walked into the house with a sigh.

The maker of toys, the great Chung-Wah, knew that all toys made in the winter are poor shivery things at best. They are easily broken, for the cross, perverse things slip out of your fingers and on to the nursery floor, and come to a bad end, very often, owing to their own wicked nature. This explains a great many things that may be seen any day in the nursery cupboard. But Chung-Wah was as wise as he was great. He made his toys in the spring or summer, pretty, laughing, gay little things, like Ting-a-ling, or polished, adventurous, gallant ones, like the Nodding Mandarin, next to whom, as you can see, she was placed in the toy-maker’s window.

This charming china Mandarin told her tales of his travels every evening before she went to sleep; and little by little Ting-a-ling began to long for a glimpse of the wide world beyond Chung-wah’s garden.

I am afraid you will think her ungrateful for this. I find it hard to forgive her myself.

​

The Dream of the Wonderful Sunflower.

**The Dream of the Wonderful Sunflower.**

​

VI.

Every night the Nodding Mandarin told her a tale of his adventures in foreign countries a long way from Japan. Every night Ting-a-ling dreamt a wonderful dream, so that little by little she forgot Chung-Wah and his two daughters, who had embroidered her a beautiful frock and taught her to walk and to dance among the almond petals on the lawn.

One night the Nodding Mandarin had been telling her a tale of a caravan crossing the desert, in the burning heat of the sun. Then the Mandarin’s voice seemed to get further and further away, and Ting-a-ling slipped off gently from day dreams to night dreams.

She dreamt she was climbing up the stalk of one of the sunflowers in Chung-Wah’s garden. It felt warmer and warmer as she climbed up nearer the top, and the light from the sunflower grew quite dazzling. At last she had to sit down on one of the big green leaves and take off the winter dress she wore when she started.

She put out her hand to touch the bright petals above her, and—what do you think?

That sunflower wasn’t a flower at all.

In her dream she had climbed up and touched the great big Japanese Sun himself!!

​

The Dream of the Japanese Moon.

**The Dream of the Japanese Moon.**

​

VII.

Another night she dreamt that a big butterfly came and tapped at the toy maker’s window, and beckoned to her with one of his long antennæ. She rose and ran towards him as quickly as her tight Japanese gown would let her. The graceful creature fluttered lower, and Ting-a-ling seated herself on his back and began to fly through the air with that uncertain wavy motion so pleasant in dreams.

Three or four other butterflies joined them, and a thin old maidish looking insect, called a dragon-fly. “That is a most proper person,” explained Ting-a-ling’s gorgeous friend, “but she won’t stand any chaff.”

They travelled far into space, until the gardens of Japan looked no bigger than flower-beds, and the Japanese Moon seemed to grow larger and larger in the sky. Still they went up, up, up, ever higher, balanced lightly in mid-air. And our friend Ting-a-ling saw that the Japanese Moon was a great yellow paper lantern. An Old Man lights it at night, and occasionally he folds the lantern up, or unfolds it, so that it doesn’t always look big and round. But that night it was all unfolded, in Ting-a-ling’s dream, and she saw the face of the Moon-keeper sitting inside.

​

The Man of Snow tries to comfort her with a little sermon.

**The Man of Snow tries to comfort her with a little sermon.**

​

VIII.

Seeing what a dejected look her face wore at times, and how the corners of her little mouth would drop, the Man of Snow walked from across the road to her window and said:

“O Ting-a-ling! O beautiful one! be not rash, thirst not to leave the shelter of thy home, where cruel boys cannot enter, and a thaw can do no harm!”

“It is all very well for _you_ to talk to _me_,” said Ting-a-ling, “about staying at home, and all that. Of course you mean it kindly, and I dare say you haven’t made the most of your opportunities, so perhaps you are a little soured and disappointed. Besides, you came down in snow flakes, and will probably turn to mud. That _is_ a come-down, I admit. But _I_ wouldn’t make any mistakes, you know, or get into any troubles.”

“Soured and disappointed! Made my mistakes! O thou rash and foolish one! Nodding Mandarin, tune up,” said the Man of Snow, “and thou, Ivory Lady, in the toy-maker’s window, sound a harmonic fifth. I will sing you the Epic of the Beginning.”

“Now then for the Beginning of the Epic,” said the Nodding Mandarin jocosely. But the Man of Snow bent towards him and said fiercely, “Brrrrr!!!”

​

The Epic of the White Clouds.

**The Epic of the White Clouds.**

​

IX.

Of course, the Man of Snow sang his Epic in verse. Most Epics are sung in verse. But, considering how difficult it is to write really good Japanese poetry, without a dictionary, I will not write it over again for you, but give you a free translation of it instead.

This is how it ran:

“Once upon a time a misty Shepherd of the air drove his flock of sheep across the blue fields of the sky.

“His flock had many sheep and many hundreds of soft, white fleecy lambs, all hurrying after their Shepherd, huddled closely together.

“They wandered after him to the East, to the West, to the North and the South, bringing dews to the flowers of earth, and swelling with rain the mighty rivers.

“They journeyed without pause.

“One of the flock, alas, grew weary of his life, and thought he would try how the world of earth would welcome him, who was a son of the air.

“The Shepherd’s Dog, a small black cloud, ever restless at his heels, barked his warnings at the fleecy lamb, his wistful warnings, or his angry threats. But in vain. The white cloud strayed from the flock. A cold, cruel wind caught him, dissolved him first and then congealed him, and he fell in snow-fragments by the road side---.”

Here the Man of Snow resumed an ordinary conversational tone.

“I was that cloud,” he said.

​

The Results of Carelessness and Malice.

**The Results of Carelessness and Malice.**

​

X.

I am afraid Ting-a-ling wasn’t much impressed by the Man of Snow’s warning. She still hoped her chance would come, and it came at last.

The winter lasts a short time in Japan. In fact there is only just time enough to get the Christmas parties comfortably over before the birds begin to sing and build, and flowers to grow, as quickly as you please.

Chung-Wah’s little grand-daughter had come to spend the day with her aunts and her grandfather. After lunch, as a great treat, she was allowed to take Ting-a-ling out of the window and play with her in the garden.

But this grand-daughter of the toy-maker’s was a careless child, and when she heard the tea bell she propped up Ting-a-ling against the almond tree and ran into the house.

You remember Ah-sid, the little Japanese spaniel who was so jealous of our little friend? He came running up to Ting-a-ling with a malicious look.

“Bow-wow,” he shouted, “my fine lady! I’ve longed for an opportunity like this one.” So saying, he slipped the noose of a string he held in his mouth over Ting-a-ling’s head and shoulders. The other end was tied to a big air balloon, as Ting-a-ling afterwards discovered, and she felt herself gently raised higher and higher, over the almond tree, over the house, away, away.

The little Japanese spaniel sat up in his excitement clapping his fore-paws, wagging his tail, and doing other silly things.

​

The Pansies weep for Ting-a-Ling.

**The Pansies weep for Ting-a-Ling.**

​

XI.

You can imagine how every corner of the garden was searched, and how that careless child was scolded by Chung-Wah, the maker of toys, by Yum-Yum, who embroidered beautiful flowers, and by Ah-Kymo, who sang love-lorn songs under the almond tree.

Ah-sid, the little Japanese spaniel, tried to keep himself in countenance by skipping about officiously, but I am afraid he rather overdid the thing, and so gave himself away. Chung-Wah’s bald head was full of wisdom and experience, and this made him regard the little spaniel’s antics with suspicion.

At last he asked him, point blank, where Ting-a-ling might be? Ah-sid’s guilty conscience did not prevent him from trying to brazen it out, but Yum-Yum, who was kneeling by a bed of pansies, heard them whisper. She picked one, and it said in her ear, “We saw her go! We saw her go! Boo-hoo! Boo-hoo!”

She looked down and saw that all the pansies had screwed their merry little faces into a sorry grimace, and two large tear-drops trickled down each one.

Now some people call these pansy tears dew-drops, but I know better. Like most sunny-natured, impulsive people, pansies are easily moved to laughter and to tears. Their own lives are always happy ones, but they take an interest in other people’s: in fact, had I to find a fault in pansies, I should say they are a wee bit inclined to gossip.

​

The Explosion.

**The Explosion.**

​

XII.

Now Ting-a-ling was about to get the very thing she had wished for so long.

Curiously enough, she didn’t feel particularly happy, and the pain in her waistband was something like the pain some children get when the holidays are drawing to a close.

I shouldn’t like to say what her worst fears were; but anyhow, they were promptly realized—for behold! to her horror and dismay, Ting-a-ling, who, as you can notice by turning to the last page but one, was travelling with her back to the engine, heard a loud and ever-increasing noise.

Swish! flap! swish!! flap!! swish!!! flap!!!

Crrbmm!!!!! (This is the noise of an explosion.)

Ting-a-ling turned a somersault and began to drop through the air at an amazing speed.

“I beg your pardon!” said an unmelodious voice. But Ting-a-ling couldn’t stop to answer. She was trying to see what kind of reception she was to meet with at the other end of her journey. For, as you very well know, there would be no danger in falling if you could only feel sure that you need never stop.

​

Ting-a-Ling disturbs a game of Croquet.

**Ting-a-Ling disturbs a game of Croquet.**

​

XIII.

“Dear me!” said Ting-a-ling, as she took a temporary seat, rather sharply, in the middle of a pond.

But the Stork (who had been the cause of this disaster, by puncturing the balloon with his long bill when flying heedlessly through the air), was following close behind her. He dashed down and rescued our little friend before she sank, and flew up again, carrying her with him, before she had time to realise what was happening.

Now a party of froggies were playing croquet on the bank at the very moment when Ting-a-ling fell from the clouds.

They are a very excitable race, as you know, in fact they have to live in watery green places, half the time, to cool their brains. Their first impulse was to huddle together and to quake visibly at every joint. But as soon as all danger was over,

“Brek-kek-kek-kek!!” said one, “what cheek, to come disturbing our games in that manner!”

“I jumped into the water,” said another, “in my indignation.”

“And I ran home,” said a third, “to look for my sword and my pistols.”

“Pooh!” said the biggest coward of all, “I wouldn’t stoop to fight a thing tied to a bursted wind-bag!” and he swaggered off.

And, hearing the foolish little creatures, somebody, somewhere, laughed.

​

Ting-a-Ling gets a View from a German Chimney Pot.

**Ting-a-Ling gets a View from a German Chimney Pot.**

​

XIV.

Mother Stork was teaching the little storks to sing, and I must own she looked a little surprised when her husband deposited Ting-a-ling in the middle of the drawing-room carpet, in their German home.

“Good gracious, child!” she exclaimed, when Mr. Stork had told her everything he knew about her. “You must take off your wet clothes, and while they dry in the sun I’ll tell you all about ourselves.

“Mr. Stork is fond of babies; in fact, whenever there’s a baby to be carried to one or other of the inhabitants of this town, he makes no more ado, but seizes it in his long bill and goes and deposits it in its cradle. You can read all about it in Hans Andersen’s Fairy Tale Book. But how did you get here?”

“I wanted to travel, you see,” explained Ting-a-ling. “I started from old Chung-Wah’s garden, tied to an air-balloon, and then—”

“Quite so,” said Mother Stork, who hadn’t been listening, “and do you want to get back to Japan as soon as possible?”

“Well, not _straight_ back, you know,” said Ting-a-ling, “but in a kind of roundabout straight way.”

“Certainly, certainly,” said Mr. Stork brightly. “We will start to-night. Meanwhile, you had better make the most of your opportunities, and do a little sight-seeing. As our nest is built on the top of the highest chimney, you can see all you want to see by sitting on the edge and just shifting your position every now and then.”

So Ting-a-ling did as she was told, and she saw the little German girls coming back from school, oh, so demurely: she saw the German boys walk up behind them and pull their flaxen pigtails, oh, so saucily: she saw the Herr Professor walk up behind the boys and pull their ears, oh, so readily: she saw the comely mammas make ready the bowls of new bread and milk for the boys and girls, oh, so soothingly; and the little boys and girls kiss friends and say their prayers before going to bed, oh, so drowsily.

​

The Sphynx in the Desert.

**The Sphynx in the Desert.**

​

XV.

Ting-a-ling said “good-bye” to Mother Stork, and started her travels with Mr. Stork.

They flew over many high-steepled German towns lying asleep, and came at last to a great sea of sand. There were no trees or houses in sight; it was a great changeless, waveless sea of sand.

The Pyramids rose straight out of it, and further away Ting-a-ling saw a great lonely figure, so still and quiet that it frightened her.

“Who is that poor lady?” she whispered to the Stork.

“That is the Sphynx,” said the Stork cheerily, for he was no respecter of persons; “she has stood there for thousands and thousands of years. There is nothing she doesn’t know, and men have died like flies in that arid desert, without her even once turning her eyes their way. The sands have risen all round her, but they can’t bury her!

“There’s an Arab on his camel looking at her now,” added Mr. Stork, as he flapped his wing jauntily—and then his voice ceased suddenly, under the stress of great emotion.

“Ting-a-ling, my child,” he said solemnly, “you and I have seen a wonderful thing! The Sphynx, I do declare, Ting-a-ling, the Sphynx looked up at you!”

But Ting-a-ling unfortunately had seen nothing at all.

​

They catch a good, obliging Camel.

**They catch a good, obliging Camel.**

​

XVI.

“My child,” said Mr. Stork, “the marvellous sight of the winking Sphynx has quite unnerved me. I am all in a flutter. My heart is beating at a fearful rate.”

“I was just wondering, Mr. Stork,” said Ting-a-ling in a kind and polite manner, “whether you wouldn’t like to take a rest?”

“You are a very thoughtful doll, Ting-a-ling,” said Mr. Stork, “and your kindness shall not go unrewarded. There are many camels who prowl about in the desert looking for bedouins and things; we will catch one and you shall ride him a little way. I am getting old, no doubt, and asthmatic. Let me see. Hm …! We shall soon see one if we look carefully; always look carefully for the things you wish to see, Ting-a-ling. Ah! there he is!” And very swiftly he swooped down on to a dark brown patch in the yellow sand, and slipped Ting-a-ling on to what she felt to be a camel’s back.

Camels are not exactly pretty things to look at, but they are good, obliging souls, and as obedient as possible. No sooner did this one feel Ting-a-ling’s weight on his back than he stretched his long shanks and began to amble along without a murmur, following the shadow of Mr. Stork, thrown by the moonlight on the sand just in front of him.

“Chu-chu!” cried Ting-a-ling gaily. (That is the Japanese for “three cheers,” you know.)

​

They met Two Little Foolish Blackamoors.

**They met Two Little Foolish Blackamoors.**

​

XVII.

I couldn’t tell you how long it took the camel to cross the continent of Africa from North to South. It seemed a short time to Ting-a-ling, because she saw so many new and interesting things.

Once Mr. Stork sat down for a few minutes on the top of a very tall palm tree.

“You can go on a little way,” he said, “I shall soon catch you up.” But Ting-a-ling preferred to stay with her old friend; and so she thanked the camel and waited quietly till Mr. Stork felt better.

No sooner had the camel disappeared round a corner of the horizon when Mr. Stork saw a roaring lion galloping and bouncing about. The fact was that two little Zulus had come out to enjoy a game of tennis in the cool of the morning, and had pitched their tennis net under the very palm tree where Ting-a-ling and Mr. Stork were resting.

“Look at them,” said Mr. Stork. “Just look at the foolish little blackamores! Do go and prevent them from dying of fright, Ting-a-ling, there’s a dear, while I fight the lion.” So Ting-a-ling did as she was bid, though she kept an eye on Mr. Stork, who, in the far distance, seemed to be ever on the verge of getting his long legs in the lion’s way.

At last the sun rose up in the east, and the lion went off to his forest bed, for no lion prowls by day. And Mr. Stork came joyfully back to his little friend, and together they continued their travels.

​

Ting-a-Ling and her American Friend astonish the Squaw.

**Ting-a-Ling and her American Friend astonish the Squaw.**

​

XVIII.

When they came to the extreme end of Africa, Mr. Stork turned sharply to the right, and after a pretty long flight he deposited our little friend in the very middle of an American prairie.

“I can provide you a little healthy exercise right off,” said a voice at her side.

Ting-a-ling rubbed her eyes. A sturdy little boy was looking down at her, with his hands in his pockets, and the brim of a wide-awake hat round his face. “You’re in America now,” he said, “so look sharp. I’m out for a day’s lassoing. Will you come?” “Yes,” said Ting-a-ling, and without more ado she vaulted on to a wild pony and followed her new companion.

For a whole long day they careered over the prairie, lassoing buffaloes, horses and wild asses. At last they came to an encampment of Red-skins. The chief looked on at their prowess in a dignified attitude, and his squaw (who peeped out from under her tent behind a mound of earth), was much struck by their feats of skill, and remembers them to this day.

If you ever meet her, she will tell you so.

​

Ting-a-Ling goes on a Fishing Expedition.

**Ting-a-Ling goes on a Fishing Expedition.**

​

XIX.

“Dear me, child, how hot you’ve made yourself,” said Mr. Stork when they met again at the close of that eventful day. “I must take you to Lapland next, to cool you down a bit.”

“I shall be much obliged to you,” said Ting-a-ling, who had learnt good manners from the Nodding Mandarin, before she left the great Chung-Wah’s house.

When they got to the frigid climate of Lapland, our little friend soon found that she would want something warm in the way of clothes. So Mr. Stork, always thoughtful, knocked at the door of a small hut, all covered with snow, where a Lap woman was sewing fur coats for her two children. She welcomed Mr. Stork and Ting-a-ling, and made room for them on a couch covered with bearskin rugs.

“You can have this nice warm coat I am making,” she answered when Mr. Stork had told her how cold his little friend felt, “and then my children can take you out on a fishing expedition.”

Mr. Stork preferred to stay at home. But Ting-a-ling went off joyously with the little Laps. They made a hole in the thick ice with a long spear, and fished in the water under the ice till bedtime came.

​

Ting-a-Ling and Mr. Stork converse pleasantly in Mid-air.

**Ting-a-Ling and Mr. Stork converse pleasantly in Mid-air.**

​

XX.

Ting-a-ling bid an affectionate farewell to the little Laps, and went off again with Mr. Stork.

Her little heart was simply brimming over with gratitude.

“Oh, my dear, _dear_ Mr. Stork,” she said, “I am having a heavenly time on my travels.”

“You are a nice child, Ting-a-ling,” said Mr. Stork. “You are grateful and thoughtful, and you enjoy everything that happens, and enter into the fun of the thing whole-heartedly. You are a most pleasant companion, and I shall not regret having taken you for this little trip.”

“What is this country we are coming to now?” asked Ting-a-ling a little later.

“This is Switzerland,” said Mr. Stork. “We shall be able to stay a few days if you like, as there is plenty to do and to see, and if we are cold we can sit in the valleys, and if we feel hot we can climb on the mountains.”

While Ting-a-ling and Mr. Stork were conversing thus pleasantly in mid-air, down below two little Swiss children, Fritz and Liserl, saw them coming, and hoped with all their little Swiss hearts that the strange travellers would alight near their own house.

​

She stands in fear of the Village Boys.

**She stands in fear of the Village Boys.**

​

XXI.

“If we are to stay here a few days, you had better borrow something to wear from our little friend Liserl,” said Mr. Stork the next morning, “or else all the naughty boys from the village school will follow you about and chaff you horribly.”

“Yes,” said Ting-a-ling, and she looked over her shoulder rather nervously.

“In fact,” Mr. Stork continued artlessly, as he shook out from under his wing a complete suit of clothes, “on second thoughts, I will save you the trouble of asking Liserl for anything.”

Ting-a-ling thanked him, and retired behind a mountain, of which there are plenty about in Switzerland. When she reappeared before her friend she looked just as she looks in the picture.

“You look a perfect pic ——” Mr. Stork began encouragingly, but he was interrupted by a loud “Mah-ah-ah-ah-ah!”

“Is it the village boys?” enquired Ting-a-ling in a hurried whisper. But when she saw it was only a nanny-goat, she said with great dignity, “Go home, you silly little thing, and learn to mend your manners.”

​

She explores every Nook and Cranny of the Swiss Mountains.

**She explores every Nook and Cranny of the Swiss Mountains.**

​

XXII.

Time passed pleasantly enough for our little friend, what with cream and honey, and mountain climbing, and other delightful things to be eaten and enjoyed in Switzerland.

Mr. Stork didn’t walk up the mountains; he flew to the top, and then called out to Fritz, Liserl, and Ting-a-ling, whenever he saw a crevasse or a glacier across their path, or when an avalanche threatened to fall their way. Under the circumstances, mountain climbing was practically a safe amusement, and greatly enjoyable.

Being good and thoughtful children, Fritz and Liserl used to pass on Mr. Stork’s warnings to other wanderers. You can see for yourself that Fritz is blowing the “Schalmei” (which can be heard for many miles), and Liserl making unmistakably plain signs to the small Swiss boy in the valley below.

On this occasion, as she was craning her neck to look over a huge boulder, poor Ting-a-ling’s hat fell off, and to her great dismay the sun began to shine brilliantly on her bright, bald crown.

​

She thinks deeply in the Stern of a Venetian Gondola.

**She thinks deeply in the Stern of a Venetian Gondola.**

​

XXIII.

After losing her hat, Ting-a-ling became a little shy of her Swiss friends. A great self-consciousness crept over her every time she saw them, and if she hadn’t been a true-born Japanese at heart, she would have longed for a wig of golden hair like Liserl’s.

So Mr. Stork thought it would be best to continue their travels, especially as there wasn’t a nook or cranny of those Swiss mountains that they hadn’t been over several times. They said “Good-bye” to Switzerland at sunset one evening, and off they went again.

They alighted in Venice a few hours later. There are no horses in Venice, no untidy clattering of those misguided, though willing friends of man, for the thoroughfares are just waterways, and the houses dip in the water and are built on islands, between which the canals go lap-lap-lapping. Everything slides and glides in the moonlight, everything slumbers or sings by day.

Mr. Stork unmoored a gondola rocked by the water of the Grand Canal, and being a very wise and versatile person, he was able to steer it as well as any gondolier.

Ting-a-ling sat in the stern and thought deeply. It is a very soothing thing to do.

​

She joins the Merry-Makers in the Carnival.

**She joins the Merry-Makers in the Carnival.**

​

XXIV.

The first sound that greeted her ears the next morning was a joyous blowing of trumpets, and singing and shouting and merry-making.

This was the day of the Carnival, as she very soon learnt, for gaily-decked gondolas glided past her, and every bit of dry land was packed with a crowd of people wearing extravagant costumes, who danced in a ring, and threw flowers and sweets at one another.

Presently a crowd of these merry-makers caught sight of Ting-a-ling standing beside Mr. Stork. There was a brigand from Albania with a Turkish fez and a tassel, a gentleman of France in a powdered wig, and a dear naughty little Pierrot who brandished his tambourine. They blew her a kiss. The Pierrot said: “What grace, what beauty! What an incomparable costume! Never have we seen anything to equal it.” (This was perfectly true.) “O Bella Signorina,” they all said together, bowing very low, “come and join our party! You shall be the Queen of the Carnival!”

So Ting-a-ling went, and everybody admired her costume and sang her praises all day. “I must see to this,” said Mr. Stork, “or she will become a perfect little peacock of conceit.”

And he did.

​

From Venice to the Black Forest.

**From Venice to the Black Forest.**

​

XXV.

“A little pastoral simplicity is what she is in need of after all this gallivanting,” said Mr. Stork to the Man in the Moon, as he picked Ting-a-ling up by the sash and flew up over the roofs of marble palaces and away, away, past the plains of Lombardy.

They crossed the Alps, and rested at sunset by a village in the Black Forest.

Here they found that the village children were having a dance.

Now Ting-a-ling felt very grateful that long ago, in that quiet garden in Japan, Ah-Kymo, the great Chung-Wah’s second daughter, had taught her to dance many dances. Instead of gazing on in a foolish manner, and feeling left out in the cold, she simply joined in the fun and enjoyed herself greatly.

“She is a cheerful little soul,” said Mr. Stork to himself, “and I like to see a playful disposition in one so young.”

(Mr. Stork, as you notice, was a prosy but kindly old gentleman.)

​

In Holland she skips with the Best of Them.

**In Holland she skips with the Best of Them.**

​

XXVI.

As they were flying through the air, Ting-a-ling caught sight of what she believed to be huge moths with fluttering wings.

“What strange animals!” muttered Ting-a-ling to herself; but not too softly for Mr. Stork to overhear her.

“We will go down and have a look at them,” he said good-humouredly. “They are only windmills, you know, and grind the ripe corn into fair white flour to make bread with, and little cakes.”

Ting-a-ling walked round one of the windmills, keeping at a respectful distance from the great wings, and presently she came upon a party of Dutch children who were playing with a skipping rope.

They had calm, demure faces, and nodded gravely to Ting-a-ling to join their game.

And this she did with great dignity, as you can see for yourselves.

​

Lucile and Auguste are baffled by Mr. Stork.

**Lucile and Auguste are baffled by Mr. Stork.**

​

XXVII.

Ting-a-ling and Mr. Stork travelled in a bee-line from Holland to Trouville.

A fluffy haired puppy-dog was running along the sand in a ridiculous, fussy kind of way, and came up barking and sniffing round our little friend as soon as ever she slipped to the ground.

“Go away, silly,” said Ting-a-ling, feeling quite angry at his unseemly antics. But the little creature gave an angry little snap. He ran off to his young mistress, and, taking the hem of her frock between his teeth, he dragged her to where Ting-a-ling was sitting.

She began to shout: “Auguste! Auguste!” and to clap her hands. Auguste came up. “Oh Lucile, my good Lucile, what a happy find!” he said, clapping his hands and skipping about. “We will bury her in our sand-castle and play with her all the morning!”

Ting-a-ling began to think matters were getting serious and looked about for Mr. Stork.

He was close at hand. One swoop, and: Woufff!!! the sand was scattered in every direction, and Ting-a-ling waved a saucy good-bye to Lucile and Auguste, who stood open-mouthed for quite half-an-hour.

​

Ting-a-Ling distinguishes Herself in the Highlands.

**Ting-a-Ling distinguishes Herself in the Highlands.**

​

XXVIII.

Away and away flew Mr. Stork, till his attention was arrested by the charming sound of a bag-pipe.

It was Fergus and Hendry Macpherson having a morning practice.

You can imagine their pleasure and surprise when Ting-a-ling came up with a hop and a skip and danced to their piping in the most engaging manner. Twenty-seven different steps she danced for those two astonished little Scotchmen, and they haven’t forgotten it from that day to this.

“And who may you be, you pert wee body?” began Fergus Macpherson.

But Ting-a-ling didn’t stop to hear the rest. She blew them a kiss with the tips of her fingers and was gone.

​

What happened in Chelsea.

**What happened in Chelsea.**

​

XXIX.

“Ting-a-ling, you’re getting mischievous,” remarked Mr. Stork, as they were flying towards London.

“I suppose travelling and seeing the world does give one some little assurance,” answered Ting-a-ling in a detached manner. “How different I feel now from the ignorant, impulsive little thing you picked out of the pond backwards a long, long time ago!”

“Quite so,” said Mr. Stork; but he smiled to himself.

They alighted somewhere near the Chelsea Embankment. Chelsea is an old-fashioned and picturesque part of London, and unexpected meetings take place there. Mr. Stork had gone for a little stroll in the Apothecaries Garden, but the over-venturesome Ting-a-ling wasn’t pleased with the calm enjoyment the Garden could afford. Half afraid of what the consequences might be, she slipped out while Mr. Stork was sampling some choice young salad leaves, and trotted along the pavement. She ran past a greengrocer’s shop, and peeped in at a newsvendor’s; then—oh, if you could have seen what happened then! Ting-a-ling stood, transfixed by great emotion, staring with wide open eyes into the next shop window. For in that window, under a swinging sign, “Ye Olde Curiosity Shop,” was Ting-a-ling’s enchanting friend, the Nodding Mandarin!

​

It all ends happily.

**It all ends happily.**

​

XXX.

The shopman—a most mercenary shopman—saw Ting-a-ling run by; he saw her stop before his shop window, and a greedy, grasping thought crossed his wicked old mind.

He took her up by the waist and carried her into his shop.

“A very pretty bit of goods,” said he, grinning and chuckling to himself. “I wonder how she came to be there! Well, well, you’ve come, and you shall stay, my fine lady;” and with that he placed her in the window next to the Nodding Mandarin.

Ting-a-ling’s great delight would have been plain to a more observant eye, for they embraced impulsively. “You dear, dear, dear Mandarin!” said Ting-a-ling. “I have travelled out into the world, and had adventures to my heart’s content. But now I have found you again I shall never leave you!”

At dusk, while the shopman was having his tea, Mr. Stork, who had come forth to look for his little friend, picked them both up in his long bill and carried them back all the way to Chung-Wah’s house.

Yum-Yum and Ah-Kymo were very pleased, and Ah-sid, the naughty chin-chin, felt the weight on his conscience grow lighter.

As for Ting-a-ling and the Nodding Mandarin, they are never going to leave one another, and they are happy together all day long.

-   sister projects: [Commons category](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:The_Adventures_of_Detective_Barney), [Wikidata item](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q34828038)

Barney Cook: a street-smart messenger boy who devours the _[Nick Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Carter_(literary_character))_ potboilers in his spare time, and dreams of making it to a detective agency. He does—but the work is not quite what he'd thought.

[Ellery Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellery_Queen), in _Queen's Quorum_ (1951) had this to say: "Earlier, as the result of having written a series of articles on the [Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Burns) detective agency, he \[O'Higgins\] saw the possibilities of depicting simple, realistic, private-eye work through the eyes of a typical American boy; his Barney Cook . . . is the most believable boy-bloodhound in the entire short-story field."

The illustrations, by Henry Raleigh, are from _Collier's_ magazine, where the stories first appeared in serial form. For the interested, the magazine is available in electronic medium at [Internet Archive identifier: colliers5019unse](https://archive.org/details/colliers5019unse)

​

EXPLANATORY.

---

In this book a number of dialects are used, to wit: the Missouri negro dialect; the extremest form of the backwoods South-Western dialect; the ordinary "Pike-County" dialect; and four modified varieties of this last. The shadings have not been done in a hap-hazard fashion, or by guess-work; but pains-takingly, and with the trustworthy guidance and support of personal familiarity with these several forms of speech.

I make this explanation for the reason that without it many readers would suppose that all these characters were trying to talk alike and not succeeding.

THE AUTHOR.

EXPLANATORY.

In this book a number of dialects are used, to wit: the Missouri negro dialect; the extremest form of the backwoods South-Western dialect; the ordinary "Pike-County" dialect; and four modified varieties of this last. The shadings have not been done in a hap-hazard fashion, or by guess-work; but pains-takingly, and with the trustworthy guidance and support of personal familiarity with these several forms of speech.

I make this explanation for the reason that without it many readers would suppose that all these characters were trying to talk alike and not succeeding.

3153298The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican — "Piggy Bank Robbery"1950Sam Singer

​

The  
ADVENTURES  
_of_  
PADDY _the_  
PELICAN  
_IN_

​

"PIGGY BANK  
ROBBERY"

​

Narrator  
Hi there, boys and girls! Paddy the Honest Pelican is paying a neighborly visit to Kenny Crow, a thrifty old bird friend, so let's join them!

​

Kenny Crow  
Caw, at the rate I'm savin' money, I'll suit enough to buy a corn field, Paddy. Yes, I will!

Paddy Pelican  
Holy doodle, Kenny! It isn't safe here. You shouldn't-You should-You should take this to the bank!

Kenny Crow  
Aw, don't worry, Paddy. I have a wonderful hiding place for the bank. Nobody'd ever find it in this secret sliding panel. See, if I hadn't shown it to you, you'd never have seen it. You'd never know where to find it.

​

Freddy  
Boy, oh boy, this is my lucky day! I've been wondering where I'd get some money, but I don't have to worry any further. I can play a mean trick on Kenny Crow and put the blame on Paddy Pelican. This is gonna be real great!

Kenny Crow  
Caw, well, Paddy, I've gotta leave for work, so I'm gonna take my money and hide it, and I'm gonna lock the door, because I've gotta make some more money to buy a corn field. I can't take any chances!

Freddy  
Aw, I can hardly wait to get that piggy bank! Kenny Crow is not gonna get his corn field if I can help it. I can't get one of Paddy Pelican's fingerprints, but a footprint would be just as good. I'll send him to jail where he can't bother me anymore! I'm not much of an artist, but this is one art job I can do. It's just a matter of copping. There, perfect! Now, with a little mud on it, I can play a good dirty trick on him. Ahaha, boy!

Freddy  
This is gonna be work! Augh! Oof! That hurt! Mm! That hurt! Mm! Wow! I'd better get that piggy bank and get out of here in a hurry. Say, that's clever! Nobody would ever find this without knowing about it. Mm! Boy, this is heavier than I thought. Kenny Crow won't get his corn field, but I'm gonna live for quite a while—real great—and put the blame on Paddy Pelican! He'll never be able to squirm out of this one. His own footprints will prove it. Hah, oh, boy! This is one of the smartest schemes I ever figured out, and there's no way in the world I can get into trouble. It's perfect! Hahahahaha, ha!

​

Paddy Pelican  
I hope I get a good night's sleep tonight. I'm too worried about all that money in Kenny Crow's house. Oof! Oh, my God! That brick just missed me. I wonder who threw it. I wonder who threw it.

Kenny Crow  
Caw! I did! And I'll make more than that before I'm through with you, Paddy. I thought I could trust you. I'm gonna get the police to put you in jail!

Paddy Pelican  
Now, look here, Kenny. I don't know anything about what you're talkin' about. I haven't done anything to you! I swear I haven't done anything!

Kenny Crow  
Do you mean to tell me-You have the nerve to stand there and say that you didn't take my piggy bank? I'm tellin' you-I'm tellin' you that you took my piggy bank!

​

Freddy  
Well, I, Paddy, say I've been, uh, wondering, I saw that bulge in your, um, beak when you were leaving his house before.

Paddy Pelican  
I didn't have any spot on my beak! What are you talkin' about?! I don't know what you're talkin' about, Kenny Crow! I don't know!

Kenny Crow  
So, you did take it, see? We caught you red-handed!

Freddy  
Well, you've got all the rights to his money, I'll tell you! I'm gonna go with you and see that he doesn't run away.

​

Kenny Crow  
There you are! Footprints, Paddy. The secret panel's open, and you're the only person that knew about it.

Paddy Pelican  
Hahahaha! This is funny! You've got an awfully muddy house, but I don't see any mud outside. Those footprints lead away from the secret panel, but there isn't any leading toward it. That just couldn't be! To make those footprints without footprints, somebody's—I have some dirty work here, I'll tell you that.

Freddy  
Don't let him talk you out of it, Kenny. He took your piggy bank. I'm tellin' you, he took it.

Paddy Pelican  
Now, listen here, how do you know I took the piggy bank? Nobody said a word about it. You didn't know. You—How'd anybody know about the piggy bank? Why did you know about it, huh?

Kenny Crow  
Yeah, how did you know about it?

Freddy  
Now, now, now, now, now, now, listen here! I-I-I-I tell you, um, uh, whoa!

Paddy Pelican  
There he goes! I knew it! He's the guilty one! Oh, boy, we're gonna catch him, I'll tell you! You—

​

Paddy Pelican  
Uh, he's running. He's running. I think he's going towards his house, that's where he's going. Hey, look what he dropped! Look what he dropped! Just as I thought. Footprints on your floor, eh? Look at this! Let's catch him.

Kenny Crow  
Come out with your paws ready! Come on out! Come on out, I'll tell ya! Come on out!

Freddy Fox  
Oh, all right. Take your old piggy bank. But don't call the police, please! They said, the last time they arrested me, that if I got into any more trouble, w-why, they-they'd lock me up for good!

Kenny Crow  
I won't call the police, Freddy, and as soon as I've taken all the coins out of it, I'm gonna let you have the piggy bank, now, and then you can save your own money. There it is! Right on your own noggin!

Freddy  
Oh! Oh!

​

The End  
—A

PRODUCTION

4258900The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican — Pirate Pete1950Sam Singer

​

The  
ADVENTURES  
_of_  
PADDY _the_  
PELICAN  
_IN_

​

Narrator  
Hi there, boys and girls! Paddy's friends, Jocko and Mary, have been thrown into a deep, underground dungeon by Pirate Pete. Will Paddy be able to save them? Well, let's find out!

​

"PIRATE  
PETE"

​

Mary  
The smoke's getting in here now. Before long, we won't be able to breathe. We certainly can't find any way out of this golden statue.

​

Captain Shafto  
Smoke rises, so the closer we get to the floor, the longer we'll be able to breathe pure air. So, get down, both of you.

​

Jocko  
Blimey—a ring like what I used to have on carousels when I was a lad in London. If you drew the brass ring, it meant good luck.

​

Captain Shafto  
Watch out, Mary! We're falling through the floor of the idle. I don't know where we're going, but we're on our way.

​

Mary  
We're in a tunnel—must be a secret passage that the medicine man used to get into the golden statue without being seen by the Indians.

​

Captain Shafto  
I don't know where the tunnel's gonna lead us, but wherever it does, it's gonna be an improvement. That brass ring saved our lives.

​

Mary  
Oh, this must be the old medicine man's teepee. Oh, we must take Pirate Pete by surprise. Oh, I hope we're not too late to save the Solar Indian Chief!

​

Mary  
Look! Look, Pirate Pete's ruffians are looting the village. They're taking everything that's made of gold. They aren't content with the gold in the mine.

​

GOLD MINE

​

Pirate Pete  
All right, men—everything—everything that's made of gold, toss it into the ship's hold, no matter how large, no matter how small! If it's made of gold, I want it!

​

Solar Indian Chief  
Have mercy. Gold in mine is enough to make you richest man in world. If you take all possessions, our village be ruined.

​

Pirate Pete  
What do you think I'm a pirate for, Chief? Whatever I have, I want more, and I don't care what your people need. I must take it to satisfy my greed.

​

Captain Shafto  
By the great horn spoon, they filled the ship's hold, and now they're pawning gold on the deck. There won't be room for their men if they keep on.

​

Captain Shafto  
All right, Pirate Pete, you're through! You can't fight me, and keep that cutlass over the Chief's head at the same time. Anyway, you're afraid of me when you're alone!

​

Pirate Pete  
Shafto! I can't waste any time with you. I have much more important things to do. But to stop any trouble from you again, I'll have you held down by two of my men.

​

Jocko  
It's no use, Captain! They've hidden our old crew, every bloomin' man, and neither Mary nor I can find a trace of them.

​

Pirate Pete  
You see, Shafto? You're beaten before you start. Don't match wits with me, because I'm much too smart! And I'll soon be sailing the brawny sea to carry my golden cargo home. And don't try to get back my golden loot. You'd be wasting your time to give pursuit, since I have the fastest ship afloat, and all you have is a no-life boat.

​

Solar Indian Chief  
Quick! Me know where he hide your men, and all my braves. We must try to stop pirates, before they get away. He make my braves put your men in gold mine, and then he make them follow. Pirate put big rock over mine opening, so the men can't come to our rescue.

​

Mary  
Oh, thank Heaven they're safe! We can't possibly catch Pirate Pete now. He's already at sea.

​

Solar Indian Chief  
You take a life boat. You go to the land of Solar Indians. My men use their canoes. We not give up while there's still a chance.

​

Captain Shafto  
At last, I see the ship! That's Pirate Pete's ship! Why, it's almost over on the horizon. I don't see how we can possibly overtake it.

​

Mary  
Well, we are gaining on Pirate Pete, Captain Shafto. I can see the ship without looking through the glasses. Why, he must be taking his time.

​

Captain Shafto  
I can't understand it, Mary. He must see us by this time, as close as we're getting. And the ship's not making any speed at all!

​

Mary  
Hey, look, he's waving at us! Why, Captain Shafto, I believe he's trying to tell us something. And I have an idea it's nothing we want to hear.

​

Pirate Pete  
Shafto, your ship is about to sink, and toss my whole crew in the briny drink. And that wouldn't be what I'd call a joke, because I've never learned to swim a stroke.

​

Solar Indian Chief  
Ah, me glad you no swim. Me enjoy watching you sink in water. Sooner than later, the better I like it.

​

Captain Shafto  
Don't worry, Pirate Pete. We won't let you drown in spite of what you've done. But you'll have to tuck all your cutlass overboard before we help you.

​

Pirate Pete  
Here go our weapons in one big shower, so, Captain, you have us in your power.

​

Solar Indian Chief  
Eh, even without the weapons, they heap bad medicine. Let them go down to the bottom of the sea, with ship. It serve them right to drown.

​

Captain Shafto  
No, Chief, the pirates can repair the damage they've done in your village. And we can return everything they've taken from you.

​

Captain Shafto  
All right, you pirates! Jump overboard! Head for the nearest canoe, all of you! We're gonna take you back to the Solar Indian mainland.

​

Mary  
Captain Shafto, you can't go aboard the ship. It's sinking! You'll lose your life if you try to stay with it. Oh, please, stay here where you're safe!

​

Captain Shafto  
But the ship isn't sinking now, Mary. I can take it back to the port alone, and without the weight of all the pirates, it'll stay afloat fine.

​

Mary  
Why, sure enough! It isn't sinking anymore. Oh, there was nothing wrong with Captain Shafto's ship, except that it was overloaded with gold.

​

Captain Shafto  
You see? Pirate Pete, your greed had the ship sinking. If you'd been content to take only as much gold as you could use, the ship would never have been in trouble. You know, gold is heavy, and the weight of all that gold was more than the ship could carry. Your trouble was all caused by terrible greed. And you're gonna repair every bit of the damage you've done, before the solar Chief lets you leave. Maybe that'll teach you a lesson.

​

Pirate Pete  
I already see I was a fool, and promise I'll try to end the plight of the Solar Indians. I'll make things right.

​

Mary  
Oh, my uncle Gabriel will never be able to pay you for everything you've done for us, Captain Shafto.

​

Captain Shafto  
Hey! There is the pelican, back with us again. Hey, that's the fellow that brought me nothing but luck, and our troubles are over from now on!

​

The End  
—A

4277636The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican — Plum Valley1950Sam Singer

​

The  
ADVENTURES  
_of_  
PADDY _the_  
PELICAN  
_IN_

​

Narrator  
Hi there, boys and girls! Paddy's good friend Big Jack Horner is broke, as all the plums have been cornered. With no plums for his baking, his tummy is aching, for plums to put in his pie.

​

"PLUM  
VALLEY"

​

Jack Horner  
You must send me your crop of plums. My business is making plum pies, and if I can't get plums, I'll be ruined.

​

Farmer  
Land sakes, Mr. Horner, how can I send you plums when I don't have any?

​

Jack Horner  
But somebody must have plum crops somewhere. It's been the same story—no plums this year. Ever since I found a plum in my Christmas pie as a little boy, I worked to become the plum pie king of Storyland. And I'd built up a fine business, but if I don't have some plums soon I'll be ruined, I will!

​

BIG JACK  
HORNER  
PLUM PIES

​

Farmer  
Well, I know where there are plenty of plums, but they're in a distant part of Storyland called Plum Valley.

​

Jack Horner  
Plum Valley? That's odd. I've never heard of such a place. How do you explain that?

​

Farmer  
Well, nobody ever goes to Plum Valley. Lots of people have gone into the place, but nobody ever comes out. That's trouble, you know?

​

Jack Horner  
But, if it's possible to get into the valley, it's certainly possible to get out. I'm gonna go there and buy all the plums, but first I'll call up Paddy Pelican.

​

PLUM VALLEY

​

Paddy Pelican  
Well, I can give you some good advice on Plum Valley, Jack. Stay away from the place. The plum trees are thick, but the mountains are as slippery as if they'd been greased.

​

Jack Horner  
Well, Paddy, I'm going to Plum Valley anyways, and I'm coming home with enough plums to keep my pie business going.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Holy doodle, Jack, not so fast! I'll go with you and help you if you get into any trouble.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Now, this is one of Plum Valley's mountains, Jack. When you get to the top, you'll see more plum trees than you've ever seen in your whole life!

​

Jack Horner  
Oh, come! Why, I'll be the greatest plum pie baker in Storyland, I will.

​

WARNING  
SLIPPERY  
ROAD

​

Paddy Pelican  
Now, the sign says "careful", Jack. The road is slippery, and it's mighty steep.

​

Jack Horner  
Don't worry, Paddy. I'll keep the truck in low gear so it can't pick up much speed.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Holy doodle! It's already skidding, Jack! Stop, before it's completely out of control!

​

Jack Horner  
I can't stop, Paddy! The road is as slippery as if it was covered with—

​

Paddy Pelican  
—grease! Well, so long, Jack! I'm getting out while I can. I have a feeling you're gonna need some help! So long!

​

Jack Horner  
Whew! I'm lucky I didn't hit anything.

​

The Queen  
Well, well, well, a newcomer! We don't have many visitors, but most people stay away from my valley. The people who do come—they like it here—least they never leave. Now, why did you come here?

​

Jack Horner  
I come here to buy myself a chock load of plums, I did, and I've got lots of money here.

​

The Queen  
Well, my dear boy, you've come to the right place. I own everything in the valley. Ahaha! Help yourself to the plums. Take all you want. Take more than you want. I'll have some of my people load your truck. Now, you may leave, any time you want. Haha! But I have a feeling you might want to stay here. There, you see? You see, you can't leave! You'll have to stay here and work for me! You can't even run up the mountain because it's so slippery! Ahahaha!

​

ACE  
TRUCKING

​

Paddy Pelican  
Okay, men, I'm going back to Plum Valley, and remember, now, I'll see you later. Now, do what I told you. I'll see you later.

​

The Queen  
My new subject Jack Horner will probably attempt to get away again, so I'd better make sure that he can't.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Ah, she's heading for the mountains. It's something mighty peculiar's going on.

​

The Queen  
Yahahaha! With a fresh load of oil sprayed on the mountains, he won't have a chance to get away! This oil will certainly come in handy!

​

Paddy Pelican  
Wow! Oil! It must be the largest oil well in the world! Now! Hey, stop that! Turn it off! You shouldn't waste oil! It's much too valuable!

​

The Queen  
Valuable! Why, everybody left Plum Valley years ago because the oil ruined the plum crops, but it's valuable to me because it makes people stay here. When the mountains are oily, they can't get away!

​

The Queen  
Now, don't you ride one up here! I'll turn this hose on you, that's what I'll do! And if your wings get coated with oil, you won't be able to fly! You come back here! If you tell my people, I'll boil you in oil, that's what I'll do!

​

The Queen  
Aw! Wretched! Blast the luck, he got away! But at least he didn't dare stop to tell my subjects how I keep them here! No, he didn't!

​

Paddy Pelican  
Jack Horner! Jack Horner, wake up! Hurry up! I flew out in the valley to got help. Now, hurry up, before the Queen makes trouble! Hurry up, now! There they are. Okay, fellas, unload the gravel now! Come on! Alright. Alright, Jack, with all that gravel on the road, you'll be able to get out of here.

​

The Queen  
Oh, I'll bet this was your idea, you wretched little pelican, but it won't work—I can still make the road slippery!

​

Paddy Pelican  
Stop! Stop! Stop! Let me explain! You're wasting all that valuable oil!

​

The Queen  
When I get through with you, you'll wish you had minded your own business!

​

The Queen  
Ah! Ah! Save me! Oh, I'll drown in oil! Get it off! Oh, you win, I give up!

​

The Queen  
You ruined everything! All my subjects will follow Jack Horner!

​

Paddy Pelican  
But you won't need to force people to stay here anymore. It's worth millions, all that oil. But I'm gonna leave now. I want to go home and get cleaned up, you see? I don't like being this kind of an oily bird!

​

The End  
—A  
MEDALLION  
PRODUCTION  
  
COPYRIGHT MCMLIV

 The following is a transcription of a film. The contents below represent text or spoken dialogue that are transcribed directly from the video of the film provided above. On certain screen sizes, each line is represented by a timestamp next to it which shows when the text appears on the video. For more information, see Help:Film.

4263987The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican — Swania Foiled Again1950Sam Singer

​

The  
ADVENTURES  
_of_  
PADDY _the_  
PELICAN  
_IN_

​

Narrator  
Hi there, boys and girls! Pelicanland owes a big debt of fifty bushels of corn to the neighboring land of Swania. The corn is all collected, and this is the big payoff day.

​

"SWANIA  
FOILED  
AGAIN"

​

Grandpa Perrywinkle  
Oh, our newest shipment of corn has disappeared. It was put in the vault this morning. Oh, why, this could ruin Pelicanland if we don't find it! Oh, we owe fifty bushels of corn to the neighboring state of Swania. And if we don't pay that debt by midnight tonight, the swans will take over our country. Oh, I'd better summon the Lord High Chancellor at once. Oh, if we don't find that corn, Pelicanland is ruined!

​

Lord High Chancellor  
This is dreadful, Your Excellency! We might as well turn everything over to the king of Swania right now! He won't accept any excuses! If you wish, Your Excellency, I can deliver the papers to the king of Swania right now, before there's any trouble.

​

Paddy Pelican  
No! No, no! What we have to do is to find that fifty bushels of corn, and pay the debt. Grandpa Perrywinkle, you mustn't let Swania rule Pelicanland.

​

Grandpa Perrywinkle  
What else can we do? We borrowed the corn from Swania, and we have to pay it back. You know, we pelicans have a reputation for honesty.

​

Paddy Pelican  
I've done a little detective work, Grandpa, and I'm gonna see if I can't find that corn that vanished.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
And I'll help you, young man. Why, with my knowledge of this country, I can show you every place where to look.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Lord High Chancellor, who besides Grandpa Perrywinkle has the key to this vault?

​

VAULT

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Why, His Excellency and I have the only keys that I know of, young man. Whoever took the corn must be extremely clever.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Ah, it would take more than cleverness to break into the vault. And, besides, the vault door wasn't broken. The vault was locked when Grandpa showed it to me.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Say, I just remembered, there is one other key to the vault. The keeper of the dungeon has kept that key, and I'm pretty sure he may have it. I'll take you to him. Perhaps he can explain where he was when the corn disappeared. If he can't, we'll have him.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Hmm... That's odd. He doesn't seem to be here. You stay here and I'll look.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Oh! Oh, I slipped! I'm afraid I locked the door. Oh, I'll have to go get the keeper of the dungeon so he can let you out.

​

Grandpa Perrywinkle  
Why, Paddy, what in the world are you doing down here? I thought you were out trying to find the bushels of corn.

​

Paddy Pelican  
I got locked in here by accident, and the Lord High Chancellor went to find the keeper of the dungeon to get the key to unlock the door.

​

Grandpa Perrywinkle  
Why, there is no keeper of the dungeon, Paddy. Why, we haven't kept anybody down here for years. But the Lord Chancellor has the key.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Grandpa Perrywinkle, I have an idea that the Chancellor did something with that corn, and I'm gonna find out. I'm gonna stay in this cell for now, and you give me your key so I can unlock the door and come upstairs anytime I want to.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Hey, I'm sorry, young man, but I hadn't been able to find the keeper of the dungeon yet. But, don't worry. He'll be back before long. And, whatever you do, now, don't let Grandfather know that you got locked in the dungeon. Hehe! Just keep quiet and wait.

​

Paddy Pelican  
He doesn't know I'm following him, and I believe he's heading towards the river. Maybe the corn is hidden at the river's edge.

​

Paddy Pelican  
It is! And he's loading it into the boat! Oh, I've gotta do something about this in a hurry!

​

Paddy Pelican  
Hey! Stop that! Stop that! You're the one who took the corn! No wonder you wanted me to stay in the dungeon! You won't get away! Come back here! Stay away from that boat! I'll get you if I have to chase you clear to the end of the river!

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Whew, that was a close call. I don't think he can catch me. But I had to leave without the corn. That makes me mad.

​

Paddy Pelican  
The only way to catch him is to fly! Maybe if I camouflage myself, it'll work. I'll take this cloth—it's the same color as the sky. That'll do it—he'll never be able to see me! I'll swoop down on him.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
I guess he's given up. I don't see any sign of him.

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Oh my! You! What? How did you get here? How did you get here?

​

Paddy Pelican  
Never mind how I got here! Just give me those oars! I'm taking you back to Pelicanland. You have a lot of explaining to do.

​

Paddy Pelican  
Why, why, you're not a pelican at all! You're a swan! You've been wearing an imitation beak. You're nothing but a spy!

​

Lord High Chancellor  
Oh, please, please don't be too harsh with me, young man. I was just trying to help Swania get the better of Pelicanland.

​

Paddy Pelican  
You're gonna carry back every sack of this corn to the vault, and don't complain about being too tired either!

​

Paddy Pelican  
Because now that you have this sack in the vault, here, you're gonna carry all of it down to the Pelicanland ship to be delivered to Swania!

​

Grandpa Perrywinkle  
Paddy, I'm mighty proud of you, son. If it hadn't been for your quick thinking, why, why, there's no telling what might have happened to us!

​

The End  
—A  
MEDALLION  
PRODUCTION  
  
COPYRIGHT MCMLIV

Two Wet Bears

The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican (1950)

The Land of More

Pirate Pete

→

-   related portals: Cartoons, Sound film
-   sister projects: [Wikidata item](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q121086904)

The narrator at the beginning refers to the central character of this story as "Tubby Round", but in the episode itself he is referred to twice as Tom. But, it is also mentioned that he bought the wishing balloon from a "little old Tom Thumbs". So, the correct name of this character is dubious and uncertain.

Key (info)

Dialogue

In scene

Storyline

 The following is a transcription of a film. The contents below represent text or spoken dialogue that are transcribed directly from the video of the film provided above. On certain screen sizes, each line is represented by a timestamp next to it which shows when the text appears on the video. For more information, see Help:Film.

4255876The Adventures of Paddy the Pelican — The Land of More1950Sam Singer

​

The  
ADVENTURES  
_of_  
PADDY _the_  
PELICAN  
_IN_

​

_"The_ LAND  
OF MORE"

​

Narrator  
Hi there, boys and girls! Paddy's friend Tubby Round buys what he hopes is a big balloon. His disappointment turns to surprise in the Land of More.

​

Tom  
Why, this balloon isn't half as big as the one the man showed me. And I thought of a great, big balloon, I did!

​

Tom  
Hey! Hey, where did you come from? Who are you?

​

Gnome  
This is your wishing balloon you bought from little old Tom Thumbs. You wished for a larger balloon, so here I am to make your wish come true. That's all.

​

Tom  
But if this is a magic wishing balloon, I don't wanna change it. I'll just keep it the way it is.

​

Gnome  
No, you weren't satisfied with what you had, so now you're going to get what you think you want. Yes, just what you think you want. See, you're a wise one.

​

Gnome  
Abracadabra, hocus-pocus!

​

Tom  
Gollee! It's growing! Why, it's gonna be the biggest toy balloon in the whole world! Slow up! Hey, don't grow it anymore! Stop it! I said stop it! Oh, Mr. Gnome, please make it stop growing! Oh, please! Please! Oh, please, please, Mr. Gnome, please! Oh!

​

Gnome  
You're getting what you wished for, and I hope you're happy with it. Ah, yeah.

​

Tom  
Stop growing! Stop growing! If you get any larger, you're gonna break right through my little house! Oh! Don't! Don't! Oh!

​

Tom  
Don't try to get away! Oh, my, it's too late for me to let go. Oh, I'm frightened. Oh, oh, oh, I'm going higher and higher! Move! You get away from this balloon! You'll break it! Get away before you make it pop!

​

Tom  
Oh, help, help! Oh, help! What do I do? Help, somebody save me, I'm falling!

​

Gnome  
Well, it's about time you were getting here. I've been waiting for you. Welcome to the Land of More.

​

THE LAND  
OF  
MORE

​

Tom  
Oh, it's you again. What is this Land of More anyway?

​

Gnome  
Why, in the Land of More, it is the place for people who'll always want more than they have. You see all this wonderful cake and pie and everything, see?

​

THE LAND OF MORE

​

Tom  
Is there more of everything? I could be able to get something to eat, then. I'm hungry. I want a chocolate soda.

​

Gnome  
Abracadabra, there you are!

​

Tom  
Oh, but this is too much. I can't even get to the top of the glass!

​

Gnome  
That's too bad. But maybe you'd like a nice piece of candy, huh? A nice piece of candy. All I've gotta do is wave the wand. Presto!

​

Tom  
Oh, but I can't even lift this piece of candy. It's so big. I can't even take a bite. How about a small piece of candy?

​

Gnome  
Don't use the word _small_ in the Land of More. Everything here is larger than everywhere else.

​

Tom  
Well, if I can't get something to eat, maybe I could at least get some sleep. Is there some place where I can go to bed? Huh? How about it?

​

Gnome  
Of course! But I warn you—there's more sleep here, too. If you get into this bed, you'll sleep for a hundred years.

​

Tom  
This is the craziest place I ever saw! You have so much of everything, that you can't use it at all. I'm gonna repair my balloon with this wad of gum and try to get out of here as fast as I can, that's all.

​

Gnome  
Sorry, but you can't leave yet. There's a great deal more for you to see.

​

Tom  
But, if I can wish for anything, I'll wish for a flight back home. That's what I'll do.

​

Gnome  
That's one wish you can't be granted, Tom. You have to wish for something in the Land of More, and your home isn't here, that's all. You can't go home yet!

​

Tom  
Then I know what I'll do. I'll wish for a parachute.

​

Tom  
Oh, my! I guess that was a mistake to wish for a parachute, huh? Help! Help, get me out of here! It's squashing me! Help!

​

Gnome  
Sorry, Tom, but I can't help you. You'll have to get out from under the parachute by yourself, that's all.

​

Tom  
But I can't get out! Oh, I'm gonna make another wish. I'm gonna wish for a big wind—a real big one! A real big one!

​

Gnome  
No, not that! You don't know what you're doing! We'll be thrown right up into the sky! Oh, stop! Oh, look out!

​

Tom  
Well, if the wind would stop, all I would have to do is pull the parachute cord and float back to Earth in safety. There! Oh, this is the best fun I've had since I met you. And I can see the Earth below us. There it is.

​

Tom  
Well, here we are. Home at last. Oh, my home is all smashed to pieces, thanks to you and this magic wishing balloon!

​

Gnome  
It's your greediness that got you into trouble, Tom. You're wanting too much! But you have one more wish, and what'll it be, huh?

​

Tom  
I wish for my little house to be just as it was before you showed up—not one bigger, or better. I never realized how nice it was.

​

Tom  
Why, my wish has come true! And it's the only wish that made me happy. I'm gonna get rid of the wishing balloon right now.

​

Tom  
And after this, instead of wishing for more, I'm gonna enjoy what I have!

​

The End  
—A

-   related portals: Children's literature
-   sister projects: [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Tom_Sawyer), [Commons category](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:The_Adventures_of_Tom_Sawyer), [quotes](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Tom_Sawyer), [Wikidata item](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q326914)

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer _(published 1876) is a very well-known and popular story concerning American youth. Mark Twain's lively tale of the scrapes and adventures of boyhood is set in St. Petersburg, Missouri, where Tom Sawyer and his friend Huckleberry Finn have the kinds of adventures many boys can imagine: racing bugs during class, impressing girls, especially Becky Thatcher, with fights and stunts in the schoolyard, getting lost in a cave, and playing pirates on the Mississippi River._  
 _one or more chapters are available in a spoken word format._

BY

THE AMERICAN PUBLISHING COMPANY,

A. ROMAN & CO., SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.

To  
_MY WIFE_  
This Book  
is  
Affectionately Dedicated.

​

PREFACE.

Most of the adventures recorded in this book really occurred; one or two were experiences of my own, the rest those of boys who were schoolmates of mine. Huck Finn is drawn from life; Tom Sawyer also, but not from an individual—he is a combination of the characteristics of three boys whom I knew, and therefore belongs to the composite order of architecture.

The odd superstitions touched upon were all prevalent among children and slaves in the West at the period of this story—that is to say, thirty or forty years ago.

Although my book is intended mainly for the entertainment of boys and girls, I hope it will not be shunned by men and women on that account, for part of my plan has been to try to pleasantly remind adults of what they once were themselves, and of how they felt and thought and talked, and what queer enterprises they sometimes engaged in.

The Author.

Hartford, 1876.

This advertisement appeared in Post-Mediæval Preachers in 1865. It was a catalog of the publisher's (Rivington's) available books.

April, 1865.

A

  

SELECT LIST OF WORKS

  

PUBLISHED BY

  

MESSRS. RIVINGTON,

  

WATERLOO PLACE, PALL MALL, LONDON;

  

HIGH STREET, OXFORD;

  

AND TRINITY STREET, CAMBRIDGE.

The Shadow of the Cross; an Allegory.

The Distant Hills; an Allegory,

The Old Man’s Home; an Allegorical Tale.

The King’s Messengers; an Allegory.

These four works are printed uniformly in 18mo., with Engravings, price 9_d. each in paper covers, or_ 1_s. in limp cloth._

**Practical Introductions to Greek, Latin, &c.**

Henry’s First Latin Book. Eighteenth Edition. 12mo. 3_s._

The object of this work is to enable the youngest boys to master the principal difficulties of the Latin language by easy steps, and to furnish older students with a Manual for Self-Tuition.

Great attention has lately been given to the improvement of what may be called its mechanical parts. The Vocabularies have been much extended, and greater uniformity of reference has been secured. A few rules have been omitted or simplified. Every thing has been done which the long experience of the Editor, or the practice of his friends in their own schools has shown to be desirable.

At the same time, no pains have been spared to do this without altering in any way the character of the work, or making it inconvenient to use it side by side with copies of earlier editions.

⁂ _A small book of_ Supplementary Exercises _is in the press._

A Second Latin Book, and Practical Grammar. Intended as a Sequel to Henry’s First Latin Book. Eighth Edition. 12mo. 4_s._

A First Verse Book, Part I.; intended as an easy Introduction to the Latin Hexameter and Pentameter. Eighth Edition. 12mo. 2_s._

A First Verse Book, Part II.; containing additional Exercises. Second Edition. 1_s._

Historiæ Antiquæ Epitome, from _Cornelius Nepos, Justin,_ &c. With English Notes, Rules for Construing, Questions, Geographical Lists, &c. Seventh Edition. 4_s._

A First Classical Atlas, containing fifteen Maps, coloured in outline; intended as a Companion to the _Historiæ Antiquæ Epitome._ 8vo. 7_s._ 6_d._

A Practical Introduction to Latin Prose Composition. Part I. Thirteenth Edition. 8vo. 6_s._ 6_d._

This Work is founded on the principles of imitation and frequent repetition. It is at once a Syntax, a Vocabulary, and an Exercise Book; and considerable attention has been paid to the subject of Synonymes. It is now used at all, or nearly all, the public schools.

​

A Practical Introduction to Latin Prose Composition, Part II.; containing the Doctrine of Latin Particles, with Vocabulary, an Antibarbarus, &c. Fourth Edition. 8vo. 8_s._

A Practical Introduction to Latin Verse Composition. Fourth and Cheaper Edition, considerably revised. 12mo. 3_s._ 6_d._

This Work supposes the pupil to be already capable of composing verses easily when the “_full sense_” is given. Its object is to facilitate his transition to original composition in Elegiacs and Hexameters, and to teach him to compose the Alcaic and Sapphic stanzas: explanations and a few exercises are also given on the other Horatian metres. A short Poetical Phraseology is added.

In the present Edition the whole work has been corrected, the translations being carefully compared with the originals. The Alcaics and Sapphics have been arranged in stanzas, and each kind of verse placed in a separate chapter, the old numbers of the Exercises being preserved for convenience in use. Other improvements have been made which it is hoped will add to its value.

Gradus ad Parnassum Novus Anticlepticus; founded on Quicherat’s _Thesaurus Poeticus Lingua Latinæ._ 8vo. _half-bound._ 10_s._ 6_d._

⁂ A Prospectus, with specimen page, may be had of the Publishers.

Longer Latin Exercises, Part I. Third Edition. 8vo. 4_s._

The object of this Work is to supply boys with an easy collection of _short_ passages, as an Exercise Book for those who have gone once, at least, through the First Part of the Editor’s “Practical Introduction to Latin Prose Composition.”

Longer Latin Exercises, Part II.; containing a Selection of Passages of greater length, in genuine idiomatic English, for Translation into Latin. 8vo. 4_s._

Materials for Translation into Latin: selected and arranged by Augustus Grotefend. Translated from the German by the Rev. H. H. Arnold, B.A., with Notes and Excursuses. Third Edition. 8vo. 7_s._ 6_d._

A Copious and Critical English-Latin Lexicon, by the Rev. T. K. Arnold and the Rev. J. E. Riddle. Sixth Edition. 1_l._ 5_s._

An Abridgment of the above Work, for the Use of Schools. By the Rev. J. C. Ebden, late Fellow and Tutor of Trinity Hall, Cambridge. Square 12mo. _bound._ 10_s._ 6_d._

The First Greek Book; on the Plan of “Henry’s First Latin Book.” Fifth Edition. 12mo. 5_s._

The Second Greek Book (on the same Plan); containing an Elementary Treatise on the Greek Particles and the Formation of Greek Derivatives. 12mo. 5_s._ 6_d._ ​ A Practical Introduction to Greek Accidence. With Easy Exercises and Vocabulary. Seventh Edition. 8vo. 5_s._ 6_d._

The object of this Work is to enable the Student, as soon as he can decline and conjugate with tolerable facility, to translate simple sentences after given examples, and with given words; the principles trusted to being principally those of _imitation and very frequent repetition._ It is at once a Syntax, a Vocabulary, and an Exercise Book.
